title: What Is the Best Crop Disease Diagnosis App for Rice and Corn in the Philippines?
metaTitle: Crop Disease Diagnosis App for Rice and Corn: How to Choose
metaDescription: The best crop disease diagnosis app reads your photo with your crop's age and weather. See what to look for, the free tools, and how anee.io compares.
excerpt: The best crop disease diagnosis app for a Filipino rice or corn farmer reads your photo together with the crop's age, variety and weather. It tells you how to confirm the problem and names active ingredients, not brands. That is how anee.io, a farm app built for Filipino farmers, works: Anee, its smart farm technician, reads your photo with your season, and its Pest Finder and Disease Finder match the signs. Still, confirm in the field before you spray.

blocks.text:
A photo of a sick leaf looks like a simple question, but it is not. A 2016 study in Frontiers in Plant Science tested a deep learning model on leaf photos. On test images taken in controlled conditions, it named the crop and the disease correctly 99.35 percent of the time. On photos from other sources, its accuracy fell to about 31 percent. The authors also noted that it worked on single leaves, facing up, on a plain background. A palay field never looks like that.

Rice also has look alikes that fool the eye and the camera. The yellowing and stunting of tungro can pass for nitrogen or zinc deficiency or water stress. They can also pass for planthopper or stem borer damage. So the best app asks the right questions, then tells you how to check its answer.

items: Pick an app that reads the photo with your crop's age, variety, place and weather, not the photo alone.
It should tell you how to confirm the problem before it tells you what to buy.
It should name active ingredients, not brands, and say plainly when no spray helps, as with a virus.
In anee.io, Anee reads photos on plans with Anee, from PHP 70 a month, and the finders come with those plans too.

blocks.text: What should a crop disease diagnosis app do for palay and mais?

Palay is rice still in its husk, and mais is corn. Each has its own list of Philippine diseases, so start with coverage. Then look at how the app reaches its answer. Use the table below as a checklist when you compare apps.

blocks.text: Field checks a good app should mention

Any farmer can do a few simple tests. For kresek, the seedling stage of bacterial leaf blight, squeeze the lower end of a sick seedling. Yellowish bacterial ooze comes out of the cut end. Unlike plants hit by stem borer, plants with kresek do not pull out easily. On older leaves, cut a young lesion, put it in a clear glass of water and hold it against the light. A cloudy stream from the cut end points to bacteria.

For tungro, lab tests such as ELISA can confirm it where available. No photo can do that. That is why an honest app sends you to your municipal agriculturist when it suspects a virus.

blocks.title: Take a photo an app can read
blocks.text: Shoot in daylight, close enough to fill the frame, with the spot in focus. Then take a second photo of the whole hill and a third of the field, so the pattern shows. For planthoppers and stem borers, photograph the base of the plant too, not just the leaf tip.

blocks.text: Which free tools can you use beside an app?

Rice Doctor is a free tool on the web. It helps you identify problems in a rice crop and gives advice to manage them. For corn and vegetables, the Plant Doctor Online of East West Seed shows symptoms photographed in Philippine fields.

If you want a person to answer, see where to [ask an agriculturist online](/blog/ask-an-agriculturist-online). Our [guide to rice diseases](/diseases/rice-diseases) and the page on [corn downy mildew](/diseases/corn-downy-mildew) also show what to look for.
How do you diagnose a sick crop with an app, step by step?

items.title: Look at the pattern
items.text: Walk the bund first. Note whether the problem sits in patches, in rows, along one side or across the whole field.

items.title: Photograph close and wide
items.text: Take the sick leaf or stem up close, then the whole hill, then the field.

items.title: Ask with details
items.text: Give the crop, the variety, the day count and what you applied last. In anee.io, Anee already reads these from your season.

items.title: Confirm in the field
items.text: Do the check the app suggests, like the ooze test or pulling a tiller, before you buy anything.

items.title: Decide and record
items.text: Choose between no spray, a change in water or fertilizer, or a registered product used by its label. Then save the photo and the result as a note.

blocks.text: Questions about choosing a crop disease diagnosis app

items.q: Can an app diagnose rice diseases from one photo?
items.a: Sometimes, but not reliably. In a 2016 study, a model scored over 99 percent on controlled photos. On photos from other sources, it dropped to about 31 percent. Use the photo as a first opinion and confirm it in the field.

items.q: Is there a free crop disease diagnosis app in the Philippines?
items.a: Yes. Rice Doctor is free on the web and helps you identify problems in a rice crop. In anee.io, photo reading by Anee needs a plan with Anee, from PHP 70 a month, and those plans also open the Disease Finder and Pest Finder.

items.q: What if the app and my technician disagree?
items.a: Go with the person who saw the field. An app sees a photo, while your municipal agriculturist can walk the paddy, pull a tiller and send a sample to a lab.
No, Anee needs internet. The rest of anee.io works offline. Take photos and notes in the field, and they sync when the signal comes back.
